exact_task.problem:
Let X be a connected compact complex manifold with a Hermitian form omega. A Hermitian holomorphic line bundle (L,h) has closed Chern curvature theta=c1(L,h), with dd^c=(i/(2 pi)) partial barpartial and |e|_h^2=exp(-phi_h) in a holomorphic frame. A theta-psh function v is a genuine quasi-plurisubharmonic function with its canonical upper representative and theta+dd^c v>=0 as a current. Because theta is closed Chern curvature, equivalently v+phi_h is a genuine plurisubharmonic function on every holomorphic frame, satisfying the submean inequality on complex lines. The function is not identically minus infinity. Arbitrary pointwise modifications of a positive-curvature distribution are excluded. For a quasi-psh function phi its multiplier ideal I(t phi) consists locally of holomorphic germs f with |f|^2 exp(-t phi) locally integrable. Write v<=_I phi if I(t v) is contained in I(t phi) for every real t>0. The upper semicontinuous regularization of a supremum is denoted by a star.

Let K be a compact subset of X, w:K->R continuous, and nu a Borel probability on K. Let V_m be a specified subspace of H0(X,L^m), in particular the ideal-selected space H0(X,L^m I(m phi)). The norm ||s||_m^2=int_K |s|_{h^m}^2 exp(-m w) dnu must be positive definite on V_m. Set B_m=sum_j |s_{m,j}|_{h^m}^2 for an orthonormal basis, and U_m=m^(-1) log B_m, with -infinity at common zeros. In the ideal-selected case the target is
 E=(sup{v in PSH(X,theta): v<=_I phi and v<=w quasi-everywhere on K})^*.
Quasi-everywhere means outside a pluripolar set. For another selecting series, state the corresponding asymptotic constraint and target envelope precisely; do not use the ideal envelope without proving that it describes that series. The weighted Bernstein-Markov condition is that for every epsilon>0 there is C_epsilon independent of m,s with sup_K |s|_{h^m} exp(-m w/2)<=C_epsilon exp(epsilon m)||s||_m.

Intrinsic section-growth dimension d must be determined from the actual selected spaces, and the kernel measure is d! m^(-d) exp(-m w) B_m nu. When d<dim X this normalization matters. The original request is to identify hypotheses producing the envelope lower bound and kernel-measure convergence and to relate the measure to a possibly nonclosed ambient Hermitian background, while keeping the closed Chern curvature. The envelope assertions fail under the explicitly supplied definition of θ-psh. Upper semicontinuity, local integrability, and positive distributional curvature permit upward modifications at individual points; they do not imply the submean inequality used in Section 8.

Take n=1, X=P¹, L=O(1), P={0}, D=[−1,1], W(x)=x²/2, and ρ=1/2. All stated geometric hypotheses hold, and V_m=span{T^m} has positive squared norm I_m(0)=(1/2)∫_{−1}¹exp(−mx²/2)dx. Here ψ_P(z)=−log(1+|z|²), with its pole at infinity, and ψ_P≤w on K.

For any finite point y and A>0, change only ψ_P(y) to ψ_P(y)+A, obtaining v_A. This function is upper semicontinuous and locally integrable, and its curvature current equals that of ψ_P, hence is positive. It satisfies v_A≤ψ_P+A globally and v_A≤w quasi-everywhere on K: a possible exception is the pluripolar singleton {y}. Thus it is admissible under the stated definitions. At y=1 it violates the claimed pointwise obstacle assertion.

Allowing arbitrary A at every finite y makes the envelope supremum +∞ there, and its upper semicontinuous regularization is +∞ everywhere. Conversely, the actual potentials are U_m=ψ_P−m⁻¹log I_m(0) and converge to ψ_P by elementary Gaussian bounds. Therefore the claimed envelope identification, matching estimate, and envelope integrability are false.

The extraction and summaries faithfully reproduce these original claims; the defect is substantive, not an extraction discrepancy. Requiring genuine local plurisubharmonic representatives would change the stated definition and cannot be supplied as a harmless correction.

Its constraint is logarithmic support growth H_Q, not multiplier-ideal comparison. notes.detailedSummary: Let X=(P1)^n, L=O(k1,...,kn), phi_h(r)=sum k_j log(1+exp r_j), P=product [0,k_j], and T=(C*)^n. Take a nonempty rational polytope Q compactly contained in int P, of relative dimension d, whose affine hull is b+W with b integral and W rational; Lambda=W intersect Z^n has rank d. Define V_m as the span of global sections z^alpha e^m with alpha in mQ intersect Z^n. This selection is exactly equivalent to the bound |s/e^m|^2<=C_s exp(m H_Q(r)) on T; necessity follows by angular averaging and separation. Thus it is an entire global Newton constraint, not just local section production. For smooth invariant w with D^2 F>0 on R^n, gradient F is a diffeomorphism to int P, and F* is smooth there. The corresponding target is the supremum of genuine global theta-psh v satisfying v+phi_h<=H_Q+C_v on T and v<=w quasi-everywhere on X. It equals G_Q-phi_h, where G_Q(r)=max_{q in Q}(q.r-F*(q)). A chartwise supremum of positive multiples of logarithms proves its global theta-psh extension, with value minus infinity on the toric boundary. Every competing v is bounded above by it: quasi-everywhere obstacle implies the obstacle everywhere; circular maximum is finite convex, has all supporting slopes in Q, and its conjugate dominates F*. This supplies the exact asymptotic constraint and envelope without invoking an ideal envelope.
notes.text:
This note fixes an explicitly selected series and proves its global selection constraint and its target envelope. No claim about multiplier-ideal-selected spaces is made.

SETUP. Fix n>=1 and integers k_j>=1. Let X=(P^1)^n, L=boxtimes_j O(k_j), and let h be the product Fubini--Study metric with potential
  phi_0(r)=sum_j k_j log(1+exp r_j),   r_j=log|z_j|^2,
in the standard frame e on the affine chart C^n. Its Chern curvature theta=dd^c phi_0 is closed. Let T=(C*)^n. Set P=product_j [0,k_j]. Fix a nonempty rational polytope Q compactly contained in int P. Write d=dim Q and assume aff Q=b+W, where b is in Z^n and W is a rational vector subspace. Set Lambda=W intersect Z^n; its rank is d. (When d=0 this requires Q={b} with integral b.) Write H_Q(r)=max_{q in Q} q.r.

Let w be a smooth real torus-invariant function on X. Its restriction is a function of r. Assume
  F(r):=phi_0(r)+w(r),   D^2 F(r)>0 for every r in R^n.
These hypotheses are nonempty: w=0 works. The ambient Hermitian form on X need not be theta or closed.

GLOBAL SPACES AND THE ENTIRE CONSTRAINT. Define
  V_m=span{ z^alpha e^m : alpha in mQ intersect Z^n }.
Each displayed section extends holomorphically across every chart: 0<=alpha_j<=m k_j. Conversely all global sections of L^m are polynomials in the z_j of degree at most m k_j in the jth variable, as is seen by changing to z_j^{-1} at infinity. Thus the displayed monomials are actual global sections with precisely the asserted selection, not germs requiring globalization.

More intrinsically within the chosen toric frame, V_m consists exactly of the sections s for which there is a finite constant C_s with
  |s/e^m|^2 <= C_s exp(m H_Q(r)) on T.                 (1)
Indeed, write s/e^m=sum_alpha c_alpha z^alpha. For support in mQ, the triangle inequality proves (1) with C_s=(sum |c_alpha|)^2. Conversely angular averaging of (1), using Haar probability d tau on (S^1)^n, gives
  sum_alpha |c_alpha|^2 exp(alpha.r) <= C_s exp(m H_Q(r)).
If a nonzero coefficient had alpha not in mQ, finite-dimensional separation would provide a vector a with alpha.a>m H_Q(a). Setting r=t a and letting t increase contradicts this inequality. This proves the exact equivalence. Also V_m V_l is contained in V_{m+l}, by convexity of Q.

THE PRECISE ENVELOPE FOR THIS SERIES. Define C_Q to be the class of genuine global theta-psh functions v, not identically minus infinity, such that for some finite C_v
  v(z)+phi_0(r) <= H_Q(r)+C_v on T.
This is a logarithmic Newton-body growth constraint; it is not a condition defined by the desired kernel asymptotics. Define
  E_Q=(sup{v in C_Q : v<=w quasi-everywhere on X})^*.
The selected series in (1) has this constraint. In particular we are not substituting the multiplier-ideal envelope from the question.

CONVEX PREPARATION. Since w is bounded on X, F-phi_0 is bounded on R^n. For any p in int P,
  F(r)-p.r >= delta_p sum_j |r_j|-||w||_infinity,
where delta_p=min_j(p_j,k_j-p_j)>0. Thus this function has a unique minimizer, by coercivity and strict convexity. It satisfies grad F(r)=p. The image of grad F is contained in P: a supporting plane to F and the asymptotic slopes of phi_0 imply p.a<=H_P(a) for every a. The inverse-function theorem and positive Hessian make this image open, so it lies in int P. Hence grad F:R^n->int P is a bijection with smooth inverse r(p). Define
  F*(p)=p.r(p)-F(r(p)),   p in int P.
It is smooth, grad F*=r(p), and D^2 F*=(D^2 F(r(p)))^{-1}>0. In particular F* and its first two derivatives are bounded on a neighborhood of Q, and r(Q) is compact.

EXPLICIT ANSWER. Put
  G_Q(r)=max_{q in Q} {q.r-F*(q)}.                    (2)
Then
  E_Q=G_Q-phi_0 on T,                                (3)
and its canonical extension is minus infinity on X\T.

First construct the candidate globally. On a chart where some coordinates are inverted, the local potential G_Q minus the frame-change linear term is
  max_{q in Q} [sum_j c_j(q) log|zeta_j|^2-F*(q)],
where c_j(q)=q_j for a noninverted coordinate and c_j(q)=k_j-q_j for an inverted coordinate. Compact containment Q in int P gives a uniform delta>0 with all c_j(q)>=delta. Each summand is a genuine psh function on the chart. The family is uniformly bounded above on compact subsets. Its supremum is continuous off the coordinate hyperplanes, and tends uniformly to minus infinity on any such hyperplane while the other chart coordinates remain bounded. Thus it is upper semicontinuous everywhere. It is psh directly by the submean inequality: use a maximizing q at a finite-valued center, apply the submean inequality to that summand, and bound its average by the average of the supremum; at a minus-infinity center the inequality is automatic. These chart potentials glue with the line-bundle frame changes. Consequently (3) is a genuine global theta-psh function with its canonical representative, finite on T and minus infinity on the boundary. Because F* is bounded on Q, G_Q-H_Q is bounded. Fenchel's inequality gives G_Q<=F. Hence this function belongs to the defining envelope class and is <=w everywhere.

Now let v be any competitor. Its quasi-everywhere obstacle is an everywhere obstacle. A pluripolar set is Lebesgue-null locally (it lies in the minus-infinity set of a nontrivial locally integrable psh function). Thus v+phi_h<=w+phi_h almost everywhere in each frame. The psh submean inequality on shrinking balls, followed by continuity of w+phi_h, gives the same inequality at every point. Genuine canonical representatives are essential here.

On T take the circular maximum
  M(r)=max_{tau in (S^1)^n} [v(z(r,tau))+phi_0(r)].
It is upper semicontinuous by compactness of the torus and upper semicontinuity of v. It is psh: rotate a point attaining the maximum and apply its submean inequality; the rotated integrand is bounded by the circular maximum. It is torus-invariant, hence a convex function of r. To see this without a toric representation theorem, pull back by the exponential map to logarithmic complex coordinates. A psh function depending only on the real coordinates has positive-semidefinite distributional real Hessian, by restriction to complex lines (or local convolution). Thus its real restriction is convex. It is not identically minus infinity and is finite everywhere: a convex function locally bounded above on all of R^n cannot have a minus-infinity value at an interior point without being identically minus infinity.

We have M<=F and M<=H_Q+C_v. Every supporting slope p of M lies in Q. Otherwise separation provides a with p.a>H_Q(a), and the supporting affine function for M at a fixed point contradicts M(t a)<=t H_Q(a)+C_v as t tends to infinity. A finite convex function on R^n has a supporting slope at every point, by separation of its epigraph. At a point r take such a slope p. Then
  M(r)=p.r-M*(p),   M*(p)=sup_x(p.x-M(x))>=F*(p),
and p is in Q. Therefore M(r)<=G_Q(r), and v<=G_Q-phi_0 on T. On the toric boundary v<=G_Q-phi_0 follows by the canonical psh submean extension, or by approaching through full-measure points in a chart where the candidate potential tends uniformly to minus infinity. More explicitly, v+phi_h is bounded above by that candidate potential almost everywhere on each chart, so submean passes this upper bound to every point. Thus the pointwise supremum and its upper regularization both equal the already upper-semicontinuous candidate. This proves (2)--(3).

This argument uses no Bergman or equilibrium asymptotic theorem. The elementary separation, submean, chart, and strict-convexity arguments above supply the required envelope identification even when d<n.

reconstruction.statement:
Let n≥1 and k_1,…,k_n≥1 be integers. Let X=(P¹)^n, L=⊠_j O(k_j), and let h be the product Fubini–Study metric. Use dd^c=(i/(2π))∂∂̄. On the standard affine chart, with holomorphic frame e and r_j=log|z_j|², put φ₀(r)=Σ_j k_j log(1+exp r_j), so |e|_h²=exp(−φ₀) and θ=c₁(L,h)=dd^cφ₀ is closed. Put T=(C*)^n and P=∏_j[0,k_j]. An ambient Hermitian form on X is allowed to be nonclosed and is not substituted for θ.

Let Q be a nonempty rational polytope compactly contained in int P. Put d=dim Q and assume aff Q=b+W, where b∈Z^n and W is a rational vector subspace. Put Λ=W∩Z^n, which has rank d, and H_Q(r)=max_{q∈Q}q·r. When d=0 these hypotheses require Q={b} with b integral. Let w be a smooth real torus-invariant function on X, and assume that F(r)=φ₀(r)+w(r) has positive-definite real Hessian everywhere on R^n. In particular, w=0 satisfies this assumption.

For each integer m≥1 define V_m=span{z^αe^m: α∈mQ∩Z^n}. Every displayed monomial is a global holomorphic section of L^m. In the standard frame every global section of L^m is a polynomial of degree at most mk_j in the jth variable. Moreover, for every s∈H⁰(X,L^m),
  s∈V_m ⇔ there exists a finite constant C_s such that |s/e^m|²≤C_s exp(mH_Q(r)) at every point of T.
Thus this bound is the entire selection constraint. For all positive integers m and ℓ, products of sections in V_m and V_ℓ belong to V_{m+ℓ}.

For every p∈int P, with δ_p=min_j(p_j,k_j−p_j)>0, one has
  F(r)−p·r≥δ_p Σ_j|r_j|−||w||_∞  for every r∈R^n.
The function F(r)−p·r has a unique minimizer r(p), characterized by ∇F(r(p))=p. The map ∇F:R^n→int P is a smooth diffeomorphism. The convex conjugate
  F*(p)=sup_{r∈R^n}(p·r−F(r))=p·r(p)−F(r(p)),  p∈int P,
is smooth and strictly convex, with ∇F*(p)=r(p) and D²F*(p)=(D²F(r(p)))^−1. The set r(Q) is compact, and F* and its first and second derivatives are bounded on some neighborhood of Q.

Let C_Q consist of genuine global θ-plurisubharmonic functions v, not identically −∞, taken with their canonical upper representatives, for which there is a finite constant C_v with
  v(z)+φ₀(r)≤H_Q(r)+C_v  on T.
Define
  E_Q=(sup{v∈C_Q: v≤w quasi-everywhere on X})*,
where quasi-everywhere means outside a pluripolar set and * denotes upper semicontinuous regularization. This is the Newton-growth envelope for the specified series; no identification with a multiplier-ideal envelope is asserted.

Put G_Q(r)=max_{q∈Q}(q·r−F*(q)). Then
  E_Q(z)=G_Q(r)−φ₀(r)  on T,
and its canonical extension has value −∞ at every point of X\T. This extension is a genuine global θ-plurisubharmonic function, is finite on T, belongs to C_Q, and satisfies E_Q≤w everywhere on X. The difference G_Q−H_Q is bounded on R^n. Every competitor in the definition of E_Q satisfies v≤w everywhere, not merely quasi-everywhere, and satisfies v≤E_Q everywhere on X. Consequently the pointwise supremum defining E_Q already equals this upper semicontinuous canonical function. All assertions hold also when d<n, including d=0.
reconstruction.proof:
We prove the statements without assuming any asymptotics for sections.

1. Global sections and the exact selection constraint. In the affine chart, a section of L^m is f(z)e^m. Changing the jth coordinate to ζ_j=1/z_j changes its coefficient to z_j^{-mk_j}f(z). Holomorphic extension across ζ_j=0 therefore forces f, as a function of z_j, to be a polynomial of degree at most mk_j. Applying this in every coordinate, or to its entire power series, gives precisely the polynomials whose exponents satisfy 0≤α_j≤mk_j. Conversely, those polynomials extend in all reciprocal charts. Thus all the stated monomials are global sections.

For a polynomial f=Σ_α c_αz^α, angular orthogonality gives
  ∫_{(S¹)^n}|f(exp(r/2)τ)|²dτ=Σ_α|c_α|²exp(α·r).
If |f|²≤C exp(mH_Q(r)) on T, each nonzero coefficient consequently satisfies exp(α·r)≤C' exp(mH_Q(r)). Set r=tξ and let t tend to infinity. Then (α/m)·ξ≤H_Q(ξ) for every ξ. The elementary separating-hyperplane characterization of a closed convex set implies α/m∈Q. Conversely, if every exponent belongs to mQ, the triangle inequality gives
  |f|²≤(Σ_α|c_α|)² exp(mH_Q(r)).
This proves both directions of the entire selection constraint, including the zero section. Products satisfy it because mQ+ℓQ=(m+ℓ)Q.

A rational d-dimensional subspace W contains d linearly independent integer vectors. Their integer span is a full lattice in W. The discrete group W∩Z^n contains this lattice with finite index: representatives can be chosen in a compact fundamental parallelepiped, which contains only finitely many integer points. Hence Λ has rank d. For d=0 the affine hull and Q are the singleton {b}, with b integral.

2. The convex potential and its conjugate. Write M=||w||∞. Since log(1+exp t)≥max(0,t), for p∈int P we have
  F(r)−p·r≥Σ_j[(k_j−p_j)max(r_j,0)+p_j max(−r_j,0)]−M
                 ≥δ_p Σ_j|r_j|−M.
The assumed positive Hessian makes F strictly convex. This coercivity gives a minimizer of F−p·r, strict convexity gives uniqueness, and its critical equation is ∇F(r(p))=p.

We also check that ∇F takes values in int P. Holding the other coordinates fixed, the resulting strictly convex one-variable function is bounded up to a constant as t tends to minus infinity and equals k_jt+O(1) as t tends to plus infinity. For a differentiable convex function these asymptotic slopes are the limits of its derivative: this follows by bounding the derivative between neighboring secant slopes. Thus its strictly increasing derivative lies strictly between 0 and k_j. This holds for each j. The gradient is injective by strict monotonicity, is surjective by the preceding minimization, and has everywhere invertible differential. Its unique local smooth inverses therefore form a global smooth inverse.

Differentiating F*(p)=p·r(p)−F(r(p)) gives ∇F*(p)=r(p) and D²F*(p)=(D²F(r(p)))^{-1}. In particular F* is smooth and strictly convex. A compact neighborhood of Q inside int P gives all the asserted boundedness statements and compactness of r(Q). For w=0 the Hessian of F is diagonal with entries k_j exp(r_j)/(1+exp(r_j))², so the assumption indeed holds.

3. Construction and canonical extension of the candidate. Let D=max_Q|F*|. Compactness of Q gives
  H_Q−D≤G_Q≤H_Q+D.
G_Q is finite and convex, being a maximum of affine functions. A convex function of log|z_j|² is plurisubharmonic on T: smooth convex approximations have nonnegative complex Hessian, and their locally uniform limit satisfies the complex-line submean inequalities. Moreover, the defining conjugate inequality gives G_Q(r)≤F(r).

Here is an explicit check at every boundary chart. Choose reciprocal coordinates in the factors where the boundary point is at infinity. If J is that set, the smooth local metric potential is
  φ_J=φ₀−Σ_{j∈J}k_jr_j,
and the candidate's local psh potential on T is G_Q−Σ_{j∈J}k_jr_j. Put
  δ=min_{q∈Q,j} min(q_j,k_j−q_j)>0.
At a fixed boundary point let I consist of the coordinates whose local coordinate ζ_j vanishes. For j∈I, the coefficient of log|ζ_j|² in q·r−Σ_{j∈J}k_jr_j is either q_j or k_j−q_j, both at least δ. All remaining coordinates stay in bounded nonzero annuli. Consequently, on a sufficiently small chart,
  G_Q−Σ_{j∈J}k_jr_j≤C+δΣ_{j∈I}log|ζ_j|²
away from the coordinate divisors. The right side tends to minus infinity when approaching any such divisor. Defining the potential to be minus infinity there is therefore upper semicontinuous.

This is a genuine psh extension. On a complex line not contained in the divisor, the missing points are isolated, and the subharmonic function is bounded above near them and tends to minus infinity. Its canonical extension is subharmonic. For completeness, the removable-point comparison follows by comparing on punctured discs with a harmonic majorant and, if necessary, an arbitrarily small multiple of log(R/|t|), then letting that multiple decrease to zero. On lines contained in the divisor the extension is identically minus infinity, which is allowed for a line restriction. Thus all line submean inequalities hold. The two-sided bound by H_Q±D also bounds the absolute value of each local potential by a constant times 1+Σ|log|ζ_j|²| off the divisor; hence it is locally integrable. The chart potentials glue by the line-bundle transitions. We obtain a genuine global θ-psh function E'=G_Q−φ₀ on T, with canonical value minus infinity on X\T.

This function is finite on T, belongs to C_Q, and obeys E'≤w on T because G_Q≤F. The boundary inequality is automatic. Notice that the curvature used here is dd^cφ₀, the closed Chern curvature of the given metric; no ambient form is used.

4. All competitors are dominated by E'. First, a genuine quasi-psh function v with v≤w outside a pluripolar set satisfies v≤w everywhere. A pluripolar set has local Lebesgue measure zero, since it is locally contained in the minus-infinity locus of a locally integrable psh function. In a frame, u=v+φ_h is psh and u≤w+φ_h almost everywhere. Its ball submean inequality, obtained also by averaging its complex-line inequalities, gives
  u(x)≤average_{B(x,ρ)}(w+φ_h).
Letting ρ decrease to zero proves the assertion. This argument explicitly excludes upward pointwise alterations of a distribution.

Every v∈C_Q has value minus infinity on X\T. Indeed, its local psh potential has the same upper logarithmic bound as in part 3. Through a boundary point take a complex line transverse to all the vanishing coordinate hyperplanes, with the other coordinates fixed and nonzero. On this line, away from the center, the potential is bounded above by C+δ|I|log|t|². The circle submean inequality at the center and then ρ→0 force its value there to be minus infinity.

It remains to compare on T; no invariance assumption on v is needed. Form the compact rotational maximum
  V(z)=max_{τ∈(S¹)^n}v(τz).
It is upper semicontinuous. Adding an invariant local metric potential makes it a genuine psh function: at a point choose a maximizing rotation and apply that rotation's line submean inequality, bounding its values on the circle by the maximum. Local upper bounds are automatic. The function is not identically minus infinity. It obeys V≤w and V+φ₀≤H_Q+C_v.

The invariant function g(r)=V(exp(r/2))+φ₀(r) is finite for every r. To see finiteness directly, V+φ₀ extends as a nontrivial psh function over the standard affine C^n. If it were minus infinity on one distinguished boundary torus of a polydisc, successive one-variable maximum principles would make it minus infinity throughout that polydisc, contradicting nontriviality and local integrability. Its torus maximum is finite above by upper semicontinuity. On the logarithmic cover its pullback is psh and independent of imaginary coordinates. Convolution gives smooth invariant psh functions whose real Hessians are nonnegative; their canonical limit is g. Thus g is a finite convex function on R^n.

Fix r₀ and take a supporting slope p of this finite convex function, so g(r)≥p·r+c, with equality at r₀. Existence follows from separation of the convex epigraph. Using g≤H_Q+C_v at r=r₀+tξ and sending t→∞ shows p·ξ≤H_Q(ξ) for every ξ, hence p∈Q. Since also g≤F, its supporting affine function satisfies
  c≤inf_r(F(r)−p·r)=−F*(p).
Therefore g(r₀)≤p·r₀−F*(p)≤G_Q(r₀). As r₀ was arbitrary, v≤V≤E' on T, and the boundary comparison was already proved.

E' itself is a competitor and dominates every competitor at every point. Thus the pointwise supremum is exactly E', is already its canonical upper semicontinuous representative, and its regularization changes nothing. This proves the asserted formula for E_Q and every envelope statement. None of the arguments requires d=n. In the singleton case G_Q(r)=b·r−F*(b), so the same construction and comparisons apply verbatim.

notes.summary: For the Newton series in n1 with any smooth positive torus-invariant probability on X, monomials diagonalize the exact weighted Hilbert norm. Elementary uniform Laplace bounds prove a derived Bernstein--Markov condition and U_m->E_Q locally uniformly on the dense torus and in every finite L^p against smooth volume. Actual dimension is d, with dim V_m=vol_Lambda(Q)m^d+O(m^{d-1}). The normalized kernel measures converge weak-* to d! times lattice volume on Q pushed to the moment-shell r(Q), with Haar angular measure.
notes.detailedSummary: The exact norm of z^alpha e^m is A_m(alpha)=integral exp(alpha.r-mF(r)) a(r)dr, for dnu=a(r)dr d tau; the monomials are orthogonal. Uniformly for q=alpha/m in Q, c m^{-n/2} exp(mF*(q))<=A_m(alpha)<=exp(mF*(q)); no external Laplace theorem is needed. Grid points in Q approximate every point within C/m. Consequently G_{Q,m}-phi_0<=U_m<=G_{Q,m}-phi_0+O(log m/m), and |U_m-E_Q|<=C(1+|r|+log m)/m. This proves the matching lower bound, locally uniform torus convergence, pointwise canonical convergence, and L^p convergence for every finite p against any smooth volume. It also yields weighted Bernstein--Markov with a polynomial loss m^{d/2+n/4}. Lattice-cell counting determines growth dimension d and mass d!vol_Lambda(Q); d=0 gives a single section and mass 1. Each normalized monomial kernel is a probability whose radii concentrate uniformly at r(q)=(grad F)^{-1}(q). Thus d!m^{-d} exp(-mw)B_m nu converges weak-* to the pushforward of d!dq_Lambda d tau under (q,tau)->exp(r(q)/2)tau. This positive measure is a lower-dimensional moment shell when d<n, not an assumed descended submersion limit.
notes.text:
Use the spaces, metric, weight, convex function, envelope, and lattice of n1. Let nu be any smooth strictly positive torus-invariant Borel probability on X. It has no mass on the toric boundary. On T write
  dnu=a(r) dr d tau,
where d tau is Haar probability, a is smooth and positive on R^n, and integral a(r)dr=1. No uniform lower bound for a at infinity is required. The norm is the one in the question, with K=X.

EXACT HILBERT TRANSFORMATIONS. For alpha in mQ intersect Z^n set sigma_alpha=z^alpha e^m. Its pointwise squared norm is
  |sigma_alpha|_{h^m}^2=exp(alpha.r-m phi_0(r)).
Consequently
  A_m(alpha):=||sigma_alpha||_m^2
    =integral_{R^n} exp(alpha.r-mF(r)) a(r) dr.       (4)
Different exponents are orthogonal, because angular integration of exp(i(alpha-beta).theta) is zero. All A_m are finite and positive. Thus the exact orthonormal basis is sigma_alpha/sqrt(A_m(alpha)), and the norm of sum c_alpha sigma_alpha is sum |c_alpha|^2 A_m(alpha). This proves positive definiteness on the entire selected space. Equivalently the original weighted norm is the unweighted norm for the smooth metric h exp(-w), whose local potential is F; its curvature is still a closed dd^c potential. This identity is only a metric transformation and makes no identification with the ambient Hermitian form.

In particular, on T,
  B_m=sum_{alpha in mQ intersect Z^n}
       exp(alpha.r-m phi_0(r))/A_m(alpha),            (5)
  exp(-mw)B_m=sum_alpha exp(alpha.r-mF(r))/A_m(alpha).
These formulas account for every norm and normalization factor.

UNIFORM ELEMENTARY LAPLACE BOUNDS. Write q=alpha/m and r(q)=(grad F)^{-1}(q). Then
  f_q(r):=F(r)-q.r
has unique minimum -F*(q) at r(q). The points r(q) lie in a compact set. On a fixed compact neighborhood of this set the density a is bounded below by a positive constant, and the Hessian of F is bounded above. Integrate (4) over a ball of radius m^{-1/2} around r(q). Taylor's formula yields, uniformly in q in Q,
  A_m(alpha)>=c m^{-n/2} exp(mF*(q)).
Since f_q(r)>=-F*(q) everywhere and integral a=1, the upper estimate is
  A_m(alpha)<=exp(mF*(q)).
Hence, for all sufficiently large m and all selected alpha,
  c m^{-n/2} exp(mF*(q)) <= A_m(alpha)
       <= exp(mF*(q)).                               (6)
This proves uniform logarithmic norm asymptotics directly; no stationary-phase, peak-section, or external kernel theorem is invoked.

LATTICE GROWTH AND GRID APPROXIMATION. Since aff Q=b+W with integral b,
  (m aff Q) intersect Z^n=m b+Lambda.
Normalize Lebesgue volume dq_Lambda on b+W so a fundamental cell of Lambda has volume 1. For d>=1, fundamental-cell comparison gives
  N_m:=dim V_m=#(mQ intersect Z^n)
       =m^d vol_Lambda(Q)+O(m^{d-1}).                 (7)
Here is a direct justification. After translating by m b, count Lambda cells anchored in m(Q-b). Cells fully inside or outside are counted exactly up to their unit volume. The discrepancy is confined to a bounded-width neighborhood of the finitely many facets of m(Q-b); its volume and cell count are O(m^{d-1}). This also proves lattice Riemann-sum convergence for continuous functions on Q. For d=0, Q={b}, so N_m=1 exactly. Therefore the intrinsic section-growth dimension, computed from the actual spaces, is
  lim_{m->infinity} log N_m/log m=d
(with dimension zero interpreted by the constant sequence). The leading volume in (7) is positive.

Moreover Q_m=Q intersect (b+m^{-1}Lambda) is within Hausdorff distance C/m of Q for large m. Choose a relative interior point q_0 with a positive inscribed radius, move any q a distance O(1/m) toward q_0, and round the moved point to the nearest lattice-grid point. A fixed lattice covering radius ensures the rounded point remains in Q. This construction works for all sufficiently large m, not only a divisible subsequence. Thus there are globally selected sections for every slope needed in the lower bound. The d=0 case is immediate.

MATCHING ENVELOPE LOWER BOUND AND TOPOLOGIES. Let
  G_{Q,m}(r)=max_{q in Q_m} {q.r-F*(q)}.
The Lipschitz bound for F* on Q and the grid approximation give
  0<=G_Q(r)-G_{Q,m}(r)<=C(1+sum |r_j|)/m.            (8)
Equations (5)--(6) imply
  G_{Q,m}-phi_0 <= U_m
      <=G_{Q,m}-phi_0+[(n/2)log m+log N_m-log c]/m. (9)
The lower inequality already uses one explicit global selected monomial approximating a maximizing q. Hence it is a genuine envelope lower bound respecting the entire constraint, rather than a local section construction. By n1, E_Q=G_Q-phi_0. Combining (7)--(9),
  |U_m-E_Q|<=C(1+sum |r_j|+log m)/m on T.           (10)
It follows that U_m converges locally uniformly on T, and pointwise there, to E_Q. On the toric boundary all selected monomials vanish for sufficiently large m, because Q has a positive distance from every face of P; thus U_m and E_Q both have canonical value minus infinity there. The extended pointwise liminf lower bound holds on all X. For every smooth positive volume and every 1<=p<infinity, the functions sum |log|z_j|^2| have finite L^p norm on X. Equation (10), ignoring the measure-zero boundary, therefore gives U_m->E_Q in L^p(X). In particular this gives L^1 convergence with respect to the volume of any ambient smooth Hermitian form. No global uniform convergence across logarithmic poles is asserted.

DERIVED BERNSTEIN--MARKOV CONDITION. For q in Q, Fenchel's inequality gives q.r-F(r)<=F*(q). Equations (5)--(6) therefore show
  sup_X exp(-mw)B_m <= C N_m m^{n/2}.
At the boundary the summands vanish for large m. Cauchy--Schwarz in the exact orthonormal basis gives
  sup_X |s|_{h^m} exp(-mw/2)
     <=C m^{d/2+n/4} ||s||_m,   s in V_m.
The finitely many small m are absorbed by changing C (zero spaces cause no issue). A polynomial is bounded by C_epsilon exp(epsilon m), so the weighted Bernstein--Markov condition in the question holds for every epsilon>0. It is proved, not postulated.

KERNEL-MEASURE LIMIT. Define the probability on X associated with one monomial by
  dP_{m,q}=exp(m(q.r-F(r))) a(r)dr d tau/A_m(alpha),
where q=alpha/m. The angular factor is exactly Haar. Its radii concentrate uniformly in q in Q at r(q). To prove this, for fixed eta>0 there is c_eta>0 such that
  f_q(r)+F*(q)>=c_eta whenever |r-r(q)|>=eta,
uniformly in q. On a large compact set this follows from uniqueness and continuity of the minima. Outside that set, use the uniform coercive bound
  F(r)-q.r>=delta sum |r_j|-||w||_infinity,
with delta>0 uniform for q in Q, and boundedness of F*. The numerator outside the eta-ball is at most exp(mF*(q)-m c_eta), while (6) gives a lower denominator c m^{-n/2} exp(mF*(q)). Its probability tends to zero uniformly.

For a continuous function f on compact X define
  f_bar(r)=integral_{(S^1)^n} f(exp(r/2)tau)d tau.
Uniform continuity near the compact set r(Q), the preceding concentration, and boundedness of f prove
  integral f dP_{m,q}->f_bar(r(q))
uniformly for the selected q. From the exact Hilbert identity,
  mu_m:=d!m^{-d} exp(-mw)B_m nu
       =d!m^{-d} sum_{alpha in mQ intersect Z^n} P_{m,alpha/m}.
Lattice Riemann sums from (7) now yield weak-* convergence of finite Borel measures on X:
  mu_m -> mu_Q :=Psi_*(d! dq_Lambda d tau),          (11)
  Psi(q,tau)=exp(r(q)/2)tau,  q in Q.
For d=0 the integral over Q is the single point, with zero-dimensional volume 1. All test functions in (11) are continuous on X. The exact mass and its limit are
  mu_m(X)=d!m^{-d}N_m -> d!vol_Lambda(Q)>0.           (12)
Thus the intrinsic normalization is essential. If d<n, replacing it by n!m^{-n} would give the zero measure. In that case (11) is supported on a compact moment shell of real dimension n+d, and is singular with respect to every smooth volume on X.

The integral-offset assumption is significant: a rational affine hull without an integral offset can have empty selected spaces in infinitely many degrees. For example a half-integral singleton has no sections in odd degrees. Our hypotheses exclude this congruence obstruction. Polytope faces touching the boundary of P and weights failing strict convexity are not covered by the argument.

correctness.report: Conditional on its declared support n1, all new claims are established. Torus invariance gives exact orthogonality, the displayed integral A_m, and the stated weighted-metric transformation. The uniform Laplace bounds follow from compactness of r(Q), a positive local density lower bound, and the probability normalization of a; no asymptotic integration theorem is assumed. The integral affine offset identifies the lattice in every degree. Fundamental-cell boundary estimates give the dimension asymptotics and Riemann sums, while inward displacement followed by lattice rounding gives the all-large-degrees O(1/m) grid approximation. These facts justify the explicit global-section lower bound, the logarithmic error estimate, the stated pointwise, locally uniform, and finite-L^p convergence, and the derived Bernstein–Markov inequality. Uniform coercivity and uniqueness of minima give the required uniform concentration of each monomial probability. Summing those exact probabilities and taking lattice Riemann sums proves weak-* convergence against every continuous test function, with mass d!vol_Lambda(Q). The d=0 case, possible initial zero spaces, and the d<n singular-support and wrong-normalization conclusions are correctly handled. Both summaries accurately inherit n1's hypotheses and preserve the scope and exclusions. The ambient Hermitian form is used only for smooth-volume convergence; it is never substituted for the closed Chern curvature. No unresolved nonroutine external premise remains.

source.report: The correctness check identified no nonroutine external premise.

reconstruction.report: Support n1 applies under exactly the stated hypotheses. The independent proof verifies all Hilbert-norm identities, uniform Laplace bounds, all-degree lattice counting and approximation, the matching lower bound, stated function-convergence topologies, and derived Bernstein–Markov estimate. Uniform monomial concentration and lattice Riemann sums establish the claimed weak-* limit and positive mass with intrinsic normalization d!m^(-d). The summaries preserve the exceptional cases and scope.
reconstruction.statement:
Assume the setup and definitions of supporting note w7-1/n1: X=(P¹)^n, L=⊠_jO(k_j), the product Fubini–Study metric h with potential φ₀, the closed Chern curvature θ, the dense torus T, the interior rational polytope Q with aff Q=b+W and b∈Z^n, the lattice Λ=W∩Z^n, d=dim Q, the selected spaces V_m, and the smooth invariant weight w for which F=φ₀+w has positive-definite Hessian. Let K=X and let ν be any smooth strictly positive torus-invariant Borel probability on X. It gives no mass to X\T. On T write z=exp(r/2)τ and dν=a(r)dr dτ, where dτ is Haar probability on (S¹)^n, a is smooth and strictly positive on R^n, and ∫_{R^n}a(r)dr=1. No uniform positive lower bound for a at infinity is assumed.

Define ||s||_m²=∫_X|s|_{h^m}²exp(−mw)dν. For α∈mQ∩Z^n let σ_α=z^αe^m and
  A_m(α)=||σ_α||_m²=∫_{R^n}exp(α·r−mF(r))a(r)dr.
These quantities are finite and strictly positive. The σ_α are mutually orthogonal, and for every selected section s=Σ_α c_ασ_α,
  ||s||_m²=Σ_α|c_α|²A_m(α).
Thus the norm is positive definite on the entire V_m, and {σ_α/√A_m(α)} is an orthonormal basis. Equivalently, setting h_w=h exp(−w), one has |s|_{h_w^m}²=|s|_{h^m}²exp(−mw) and ||s||_m²=∫_X|s|_{h_w^m}²dν. The local potential of h_w is F, and its Chern curvature is the closed form θ+dd^cw; it is not identified with an ambient Hermitian form.

For this orthonormal basis define B_m=Σ_α|σ_α|_{h^m}²/A_m(α) and U_m=m^−1log B_m, with value −∞ at common zeros. On T the exact identities are
  B_m(r)=Σ_{α∈mQ∩Z^n} exp(α·r−mφ₀(r))/A_m(α),
  exp(−mw(r))B_m(r)=Σ_{α∈mQ∩Z^n} exp(α·r−mF(r))/A_m(α).
There is a constant c>0 such that for all sufficiently large m and every selected α, with q=α/m,
  c m^−n/2 exp(mF*(q))≤A_m(α)≤exp(mF*(q)).
These bounds are uniform in the selected q∈Q and give uniform logarithmic norm asymptotics.

Normalize relative Lebesgue measure dq_Λ on b+W so that a fundamental cell of Λ has volume 1, and write vol_Λ(Q)=∫_Qdq_Λ. For d=0 give the singleton volume 1. One has (m aff Q)∩Z^n=mb+Λ. If d≥1, the actual selected dimension is
  N_m:=dim V_m=#(mQ∩Z^n)=m^d vol_Λ(Q)+O(m^{d−1}),
where vol_Λ(Q)>0. If d=0, N_m=1 for every m. In particular, V_m is nonzero for every sufficiently large m, and the intrinsic section-growth dimension is
  lim_{m→∞}log N_m/log m=d.
For every continuous g:Q→R,
  m^−d Σ_{α∈mQ∩Z^n}g(α/m)→∫_Qg(q)dq_Λ.
Furthermore, Q_m:=Q∩(b+m^−1Λ) has Hausdorff distance at most C/m from Q for all sufficiently large m, with a constant C independent of m; this holds for all sufficiently large degrees, not only a divisible subsequence. For d=0, Q_m=Q.

For sufficiently large m put G_{Q,m}(r)=max_{q∈Q_m}(q·r−F*(q)). There are constants independent of m and r such that on R^n
  0≤G_Q(r)−G_{Q,m}(r)≤C(1+Σ_j|r_j|)/m,
and on T
  G_{Q,m}−φ₀≤U_m≤G_{Q,m}−φ₀+[(n/2)log m+log N_m−log c]/m.
Consequently, for all sufficiently large m and every point of T,
  |U_m−E_Q|≤C(1+Σ_j|r_j|+log m)/m.
In particular U_m→E_Q locally uniformly and pointwise on T. All selected monomials vanish on X\T for sufficiently large m, so U_m and E_Q both have canonical value −∞ there. The extended pointwise lower bound liminf_{m→∞}U_m≥E_Q holds everywhere on X, and there is extended-real pointwise convergence everywhere. For every smooth positive volume measure on X and every 1≤p<∞, U_m→E_Q in L^p with respect to that measure, hence also in L¹ with respect to the volume of any smooth ambient Hermitian form. No global uniform convergence across the logarithmic poles is asserted.

There is a constant C, independent of m and s, such that for all sufficiently large m
  sup_X exp(−mw)B_m≤C N_m m^{n/2},
and, after absorbing the finitely many small degrees into the constant,
  sup_X |s|_{h^m}exp(−mw/2)≤C m^{d/2+n/4}||s||_m  for every m≥1 and s∈V_m.
Thus for every ε>0 there is C_ε independent of m and s with
  sup_X |s|_{h^m}exp(−mw/2)≤C_ε exp(εm)||s||_m.
The weighted Bernstein–Markov condition therefore holds.

For α∈mQ∩Z^n, q=α/m, define a probability P_{m,q} on T, extended by zero to X\T, by
  dP_{m,q}=exp(m(q·r−F(r)))a(r)dr dτ/A_m(α).
Its angular factor is exactly Haar probability. With f_q(r)=F(r)−q·r, for every η>0 there is c_η>0 such that
  f_q(r)+F*(q)≥c_η
for every q∈Q and every r with |r−r(q)|≥η. The radial probabilities concentrate uniformly at r(q):
  sup_{q∈Q_m}P_{m,q}({|r−r(q)|≥η})→0  for every η>0.
For any continuous f:X→R put f̄(r)=∫_{(S¹)^n}f(exp(r/2)τ)dτ. Then
  sup_{q∈Q_m}|∫_Xf dP_{m,q}−f̄(r(q))|→0.

The finite Borel kernel measures satisfy the exact identity
  μ_m:=d!m^−d exp(−mw)B_mν=d!m^−d Σ_{α∈mQ∩Z^n}P_{m,α/m}.
They converge weak-* against every continuous function on X to
  μ_Q=Ψ_*(d!dq_Λ dτ),  Ψ(q,τ)=exp(r(q)/2)τ,  (q,τ)∈Q×(S¹)^n.
Their masses satisfy
  μ_m(X)=d!m^−dN_m→d!vol_Λ(Q)>0.
For d=0 this means mass 1 and Haar probability on the single torus with radii r(b). If d<n, the measures normalized instead by n!m^−n converge weak-* to zero. In that case μ_Q is supported on the compact shell Ψ(Q×(S¹)^n), of real dimension n+d, and is singular with respect to every smooth ambient volume.

The integral-affine-offset assumption is part of the theorem. Without it, a rational affine hull can produce empty spaces in infinitely many degrees; for example, a rational singleton with a half-integral coordinate has no selected section in odd degrees. The claims above do not cover polytopes meeting the boundary of P or weights for which the stipulated strict convexity of F fails.
reconstruction.proof:
We use the conclusions of w7-1/n1, whose hypotheses are exactly those assumed here. All estimates below are derived from the displayed integrals, rather than from a Bergman asymptotic theorem.

1. The entire Hilbert space and its norm. The boundary X\T is a finite union of smooth coordinate divisors and has zero mass for any smooth volume. In polar coordinates the invariant smooth positive probability ν has the form a(r)dr dτ, with a smooth and strictly positive, ∫a=1, and dτ Haar probability. Since w and the metric are invariant, angular Fourier orthogonality gives
  A_m(α)=∫ exp(m(q·r−F(r)))a(r)dr,  q=α/m,
  ||Σ_α c_ασ_α||²_m=Σ_α|c_α|²A_m(α).
Each monomial is a nonzero global section by n1. Its integral is finite by compactness and is positive since ν is strictly positive. These formulas prove positive definiteness on the whole selected space and give the asserted orthonormal basis. They include every selected section, not just individual monomials.

Multiplying the metric by exp(−w) gives h_w with |s|²_{h_w^m}=|s|²_{h^m}exp(−mw). Its local potential is φ₀+w=F and its curvature is θ+dd^cw, which is closed. Thus the asserted Hilbert-norm transformation is exact. It makes no reference to an ambient Hermitian form. Substitution of the orthonormal monomials gives both exact formulas for B_m and exp(−mw)B_m.

2. Uniform logarithmic Laplace estimates. Put f_q(r)=F(r)−q·r and R_Q={r(q):q∈Q}. By n1, R_Q is compact, f_q has its unique minimum −F*(q) at r(q), and F* is bounded on Q. Since ∫a=1,
  A_m(α)≤exp(mF*(q)).
On a fixed small neighborhood of R_Q, a has a positive minimum and D²F has a finite upper bound. Taylor's formula, whose linear term vanishes at r(q), gives uniformly
  0≤f_q(r(q)+u)+F*(q)≤C|u|²
for sufficiently small u. Integrating over |u|≤m^{−1/2} yields
  A_m(α)≥c m^{−n/2}exp(mF*(q))
for all sufficiently large m, with c>0 independent of q∈Q. In particular these estimates do not require a lower bound on a at infinity. The proof applies even to real q∈Q when the same integral is considered without a section interpretation.

3. Counting the actual spaces, in every sufficiently large degree. Since b is integral,
  (m aff Q)∩Z^n=mb+Λ,
and therefore Q_m=Q∩(b+m^{−1}Λ). Work in the affine space b+W with lattice-normalized volume. When d≥1, Q has a relative interior ball B_W(q₀,ρ)⊂Q. Let R be a covering radius of Λ, so every point of b+W is within R/m of b+m^{−1}Λ. For q∈Q, move it to
  x=(1−t)q+tq₀,  t=2R/(mρ).
For large m, 0<t≤1 and B_W(x,tρ)⊂Q by convexity. A nearest grid point y consequently belongs to Q and satisfies
  |y−q|≤t diam(Q)+R/m≤C/m.
Since Q_m⊂Q, this proves the claimed Hausdorff estimate and nonemptiness for every sufficiently large m, not just a subsequence.

Choose bounded fundamental cells of the scaled lattice, each of volume m^{−d}. The union of the cells based at Q_m differs from Q only in a strip of width C/m about ∂Q. A bounded polytope has strip volume O(1/m): its boundary has finitely many faces, each lying in a hyperplane, and each strip is contained in a bounded slab of that width. Taking volumes yields
  m^{−d}#Q_m=vol_Λ(Q)+O(1/m).
This proves N_m=m^dvol_Λ(Q)+O(m^{d−1}). For continuous g on Q, the same cells give the Riemann-sum formula. For example, extend g continuously to a neighborhood by composing it with nearest-point projection onto Q. Uniform continuity makes the error on every cell tend uniformly to zero; the boundary-strip contribution also tends to zero. Hence
  m^{−d}Σ_{q∈Q_m}g(q)→∫_Q g dq_Λ.
The leading volume is strictly positive because Q has dimension d. Thus log N_m/log m→d. If d=0, Q={b}, the integral offset makes mb integral for every m, and N_m=1, Q_m=Q, with counting volume 1. All the formulas have the specified singleton interpretation.

4. The envelope lower bound and all function convergence statements. F* is Lipschitz on Q. The Hausdorff estimate, applied to a maximizing q for G_Q(r), gives
  0≤G_Q(r)−G_{Q,m}(r)≤C(1+|r|)/m.
For the exact kernel sum, the upper estimate for A_m implies that its largest individual term is at least exp(m(G_{Q,m}−φ₀)). The lower estimate for A_m bounds every term from above by c^{−1}m^{n/2} times that same largest exponential. Therefore
  G_{Q,m}−φ₀≤U_m≤G_{Q,m}−φ₀+[(n/2)log m+log N_m−log c]/m.
Using the counting bound and E_Q=G_Q−φ₀ from n1 gives the stated uniform-in-r estimate
  |U_m−E_Q|≤C(1+Σ_j|r_j|+log m)/m.
The sections providing the lower estimate are the actual globally defined selected monomials. Their entire selection constraint was proved in n1; no local section or unproved globalization is involved.

This proves locally uniform and pointwise convergence on T. There is δ>0 with δ≤q_j≤k_j−δ for every q∈Q. Every selected exponent therefore satisfies α_j>0 and mk_j−α_j>0. The corresponding monomial vanishes at both boundary points of each factor. Thus, once the spaces are nonempty, all selected monomials vanish on X\T, and U_m there has its genuine canonical value minus infinity. The same is true of E_Q by n1. We obtain extended-real pointwise convergence on all X and in particular liminf U_m≥E_Q everywhere.

For a smooth positive volume measure on X, every |r_j| has every finite moment. Indeed, near zero or infinity it is the absolute value of a constant multiple of log|ζ_j|, and ∫_0^ε |log t|^p t dt is finite. Finite product charts prove this for any smooth volume. Also E_Q itself is bounded in absolute value on T by C(1+Σ|r_j|), using |G_Q−H_Q|≤C and the elementary bounds on φ₀ and H_Q. The displayed error estimate now yields L^p convergence for every 1≤p<∞, in fact an O((1+log m)/m) bound for the L^p norm of the difference. Values on the divisors are ignored in these almost-everywhere representatives. This includes the volume of every smooth ambient Hermitian form. No global uniform assertion at the poles follows or is needed.

5. Bernstein–Markov. For q∈Q the exponential exp(m(q·r−F(r))) is everywhere at most exp(mF*(q)). The lower bound for A_m consequently gives
  exp(−mw)B_m≤c^{−1}N_m m^{n/2}
throughout T and, by continuity and the boundary vanishing, throughout X for large m. Evaluation followed by Cauchy–Schwarz in the orthonormal basis gives, for every s∈V_m,
  |s(x)|_{h^m}exp(−mw(x)/2)≤[exp(−mw(x))B_m(x)]^{1/2}||s||_m.
Since N_m≤C m^d, this is the asserted polynomial estimate. Each of the finitely many smaller spaces has a finite evaluation bound on compact X; zero spaces cause no problem. Absorbing these bounds gives one constant valid for every m. Finally any fixed polynomial is bounded by C_ε exp(εm), proving the weighted Bernstein–Markov condition with exactly the requested norm and weight.

6. Uniform concentration and the kernel measure. The same δ gives
  f_q(r)+F*(q)≥δΣ|r_j|−C
uniformly for q∈Q. Outside a fixed compact set this is bounded below by a positive constant. On that compact set, the continuous function f_q(r)+F*(q) is nonnegative and vanishes only at r=r(q). Thus, restricting to |r−r(q)|≥η gives a strictly positive minimum. Combining the two regions proves the stated c_η>0 for all q∈Q and all such r.

The probability P_{m,q} has exactly Haar angular factor. On its radial complement of the η-ball its numerator integral is at most exp(mF*(q)−mc_η)∫a, whereas its denominator is at least c m^{−n/2}exp(mF*(q)). Hence
  P_{m,q}(|r−r(q)|≥η)≤c^{−1}m^{n/2}exp(−mc_η),
uniformly on Q_m. This proves the required concentration without assumptions on density at infinity.

For f∈C(X), the angular average f̄ is continuous. On a compact neighborhood of R_Q it is uniformly continuous. Splitting the integral into the η-ball and its complement gives
  |∫f dP_{m,q}−f̄(r(q))|≤ω(η)+2||f||∞ c^{−1}m^{n/2}exp(−mc_η),
where ω(η)→0. First let m→∞ and then η→0. This proves the uniform test-function statement.

The formula for the kernel gives the exact identity of finite positive measures
  μ_m=d!m^{−d}Σ_{q∈Q_m}P_{m,q}.
Therefore μ_m(X)=d!m^{−d}N_m. For a continuous test function f, the difference between μ_m(f) and
  d!m^{−d}Σ_{q∈Q_m}f̄(r(q))
tends to zero, since m^{−d}N_m stays bounded and the preceding errors are uniform. The Riemann-sum statement then gives
  μ_m(f)→d!∫_Q∫_{(S¹)^n}f(exp(r(q)/2)τ)dτ dq_Λ.
This is precisely weak-* convergence to Ψ_*(d!dq_Λ dτ), with limiting mass d!vol_Λ(Q)>0. In dimension zero it is Haar probability on the one torus of radii r(b).

For d<n, normalization by n!m^{−n} multiplies μ_m by (n!/d!)m^{d−n}; hence those measures converge weak-* to zero. The map q↦r(q) is injective and has injective differential on W, and polar coordinates separate radial and angular variables. Thus Ψ is an embedding on the relative interior and on each face, with top real dimension d+n. The image of the compact domain is compact. Every neighborhood of each domain point has positive relative-volume-times-Haar measure, so this compact image is exactly the support of μ_Q. Its finitely many face strata all have dimension at most n+d<2n. Local submanifold charts, or graph charts and Fubini, show that their ambient smooth volumes vanish. Consequently μ_Q is singular with respect to every smooth ambient volume.

Finally, the lattice-offset condition was used explicitly for (m aff Q)∩Z^n=mb+Λ and all-degree grid approximation. Without it, a singleton with a half-integral coordinate has no integral exponent in odd degrees. The argument deliberately does not address boundary-touching Q or failure of strict convexity. This completes every assertion of the note.

notes.summary: Complete new sufficient-condition theorem for sparse interior Newton-polytope series on (P1)^n, including intrinsic d<n growth, explicit global lower bound, proved BM, and weak-* moment-shell kernel limit. It is not an ideal-series or arbitrary-series theorem. The limit has a precise induced-volume density for any ambient Hermitian form; for d<n it cannot be an ambient mixed Monge--Ampere measure. For d=n it is the nonpluripolar closed-curvature MA measure. An explicit O(4,4) rank-one series with rational-map base points and a nonclosed sampling Hermitian background demonstrates a case not given by a submersion pullback.
notes.detailedSummary: Combining n1 and n2 gives a fully proved condition-finding answer: X=(P1)^n, product Fubini--Study h on O(k1,...,kn), K=X, smooth invariant w with D^2(phi_h+w)>0, smooth positive invariant probability nu, and V_m exactly the monomial space for a nonempty interior rational polytope Q with aff Q=b+W, integral b and rational W. The target is the global theta-psh Newton-growth envelope, not the multiplier-ideal envelope. Actual growth dimension is dim Q, mass d!vol_Lambda Q is positive, potentials converge locally uniformly on the torus and in every finite L^p against smooth volume, and normalized measures converge weak-* to Psi_*(d!dq_Lambda d tau). For arbitrary Hermitian omega, pullback of induced Riemannian volume on the shell under Psi is J_omega dq_Lambda d tau; consequently dmu_Q=(d!/J_omega)dvol_{omega,shell}. This allows nonclosed omega without changing the closed theta. Locally G_Q is C^{1,1}, with Hessian rank at most d, so for d<n its nonpluripolar (d+1)st curvature power is zero and any smooth-ambient mixed dth measure is absolutely continuous on the torus, unlike the positive singular kernel limit. For d=n, direct Hessian calculation proves mu_Q=<(theta+dd^c E_Q)^n>. The example Q={(2+t,2-t): |t|<=1/2} in O(4,4) has N_m=2 floor(m/2)+1 and mass 1, with limit supported on |z1 z2|=1 and explicitly specified radii. The projective ratio is z1/z2 with indeterminacy points, not a global submersion; the norms exhibit concentration in a transverse radial direction. Non-invariant sampling, nonconvex weights, boundary polytopes, arbitrary multiplier-ideal spaces, and arbitrary selecting series remain outside the theorem.
notes.text:
COMPLETE SCOPED SUFFICIENT-CONDITION ANSWER.

The following theorem is a condition-finding solution, not a universal theorem for multiplier ideals or selecting series. Its primary nontrivial cases have n>=2 and 1<=d<n. They are sparse globally constrained section series with transverse radial concentration, not merely a restatement of a positive-mass big-line-bundle theorem or a descended submersion limit.

THEOREM. Assume all of the following explicit conditions.
(1) X=(P^1)^n; L=boxtimes O(k_j), k_j positive integers; h is the product Fubini--Study metric. In the dense torus T=(C*)^n write r_j=log|z_j|^2 and phi_0=sum k_j log(1+exp r_j). Thus theta=c_1(L,h)=dd^c phi_0 is closed. The ambient Hermitian form omega may be nonclosed.
(2) K=X. The obstacle w is smooth and torus-invariant, and F=phi_0+w has positive-definite real Hessian at every r in R^n.
(3) nu is a smooth strictly positive torus-invariant probability on X. In particular one may take nu=omega^n/integral_X omega^n when omega is a torus-invariant Hermitian form, whether or not omega is closed. For a non-invariant omega, an independent invariant nu is allowed, but its volume is not asserted to satisfy (3).
(4) Q is a nonempty rational polytope compactly contained in the interior of P=product [0,k_j]. Its affine hull is b+W with b in Z^n and W rational. The specified selection is exactly
  V_m=span{z^alpha e^m : alpha in mQ intersect Z^n}.
Set Lambda=W intersect Z^n and normalize relative volume dq_Lambda by covolume 1. Put d=dim Q.

For this series the precise target is
  E_Q=(sup{v genuine global theta-psh, v+phi_0<=H_Q+C_v on T
                 for some finite C_v, and v<=w q.e. on X})^*,
where H_Q(r)=max_{q in Q} q.r. It is not the ideal envelope unless some separate argument proves such an identification. Let F* be the convex conjugate on int P and r(q)=(grad F)^{-1}(q). Then
  E_Q= max_{q in Q}[q.r-F*(q)]-phi_0 on T,
with canonical value minus infinity on X\T.

The weighted norm is positive definite on V_m. Its weighted Bernstein--Markov condition is valid. The actual dimensions satisfy
  dim V_m=m^d vol_Lambda(Q)+O(m^{d-1}) for d>=1,
and dim V_m=1 for d=0. Therefore d is the intrinsic section-growth dimension, not automatically dim X. For the orthonormal kernel in the question,
  U_m -> E_Q locally uniformly on T,
  U_m -> E_Q in L^p(X,dvol_omega) for every 1<=p<infinity,
and the extended pointwise envelope lower bound liminf U_m>=E_Q holds on X. In fact there is two-sided convergence on T and canonical minus-infinity values on the toric boundary for large m.

The finite Borel kernel measures converge weak-* (against every continuous test function on X):
  d!m^{-d} exp(-mw)B_m nu -> mu_Q,
  mu_Q=Psi_*(d!dq_Lambda d tau),
  Psi(q,tau)=exp(r(q)/2)tau.
Their limiting mass is d!vol_Lambda(Q)>0. When d=0 the volume of the singleton is 1 and the limit is Haar probability on one n-dimensional real torus. When d<n the n-dimensional normalization would instead yield zero.

PROOF OF THE ANALYTIC AND GLOBALIZATION CLAIMS. All of these assertions, including the exact target identification, are proved in n1 and n2. In particular n1 proves the global section space and exact equivalence between selection and the bound |s/e^m|^2<=C_s exp(mH_Q). It also proves the envelope formula using the circular maximum of each genuine psh competitor, rather than assuming competitors invariant. Its chart construction proves a genuine global theta-psh candidate, with no pointwise representative changes. In n2 the exact orthogonal basis, all norm transformations, and the elementary uniform estimates
  c m^{-n/2} exp(mF*(alpha/m)) <= ||z^alpha e^m||_m^2
             <= exp(mF*(alpha/m))
are established. A lattice grid approximation supplies global selected sections for every maximizing slope. The resulting estimate
  |U_m-E_Q|<=C(1+sum |r_j|+log m)/m
proves the stated topologies. Counting the actual selected lattice points establishes the intrinsic dimension and normalization. Finally individual monomial probabilities concentrate uniformly at r(alpha/m), and lattice Riemann sums prove the stated limit. These arguments do not assume any desired kernel asymptotic or rely on an external Bergman, toric quantization, or Monge--Ampere asymptotic theorem.

RELATION TO AN ARBITRARY AMBIENT HERMITIAN FORM. Let g_omega(u,v)=omega(u,Jv), with Riemannian volume dvol_omega=omega^n/n!. For d>=1 disregard the relative boundary of Q, which has zero dq_Lambda measure. The image
  S_Q=Psi(relint Q x (S^1)^n)
is a smooth embedded real submanifold of dimension n+d. Indeed grad F is a diffeomorphism, so its inverse restricted to aff Q is an immersion and embedding; angular coordinates give the additional n independent directions. For d=0 use the single embedded torus. Let dvol_{omega,S_Q} be the induced Riemannian volume. There is a unique smooth positive Jacobian J_omega satisfying
  Psi^*(dvol_{omega,S_Q})=J_omega(q,tau)dq_Lambda d tau.
Consequently the exact geometric density relation is
  dmu_Q=(d!/J_omega)dvol_{omega,S_Q} on S_Q.          (13)
No closedness of omega is required in this statement. It follows just by change of variables on an embedded submanifold. This is a direct and precise relation of the limit to a possibly nonclosed background; it does not replace theta by omega. The limit is independent of the choice of smooth positive invariant nu, although the Hilbert norms themselves depend on that choice.

For d<n, (13) is a submanifold density, not a density with respect to omega^n. The support S_Q has real codimension n-d>0 and mu_Q is singular with respect to smooth ambient volume. In particular there is no justification for identifying it with a universal mixed measure involving a nonclosed omega.

CLOSED-CURVATURE IDENTIFICATION AND THE LOWER-DIMENSIONAL OBSTRUCTION. These claims can also be made precise without importing an external asymptotic theorem. Put G=G_Q. On Q the conjugate F* is uniformly strongly convex in W. Hence the maximizer q(r) in the definition of G is unique. The variational inequalities at q(r) and q(s) imply
  (r-s).(q(r)-q(s))
     >=(grad F*(q(r))-grad F*(q(s))).(q(r)-q(s))
     >=c|q(r)-q(s)|^2.
Thus q(r) is Lipschitz. Comparing the optimizing values at r and r+h shows grad G=q(r), so G is C^{1,1}. Since its gradient takes values in b+W, its almost-everywhere Hessian has rank at most d. On T the closed curvature current of the envelope is
  T_Q=theta+dd^c E_Q=dd^c G.
The local bounded-psh powers of this current are given by Hessian minors. For completeness, mollify G in r on a relatively compact logarithmic chart. The mollifications are smooth convex, converge in C^1, and have uniformly bounded Hessian. Their Hessians converge almost everywhere and locally in finite L^p to the weak Hessian of G. All minors therefore converge in L^1. The corresponding wedge currents converge to those minors; the identity with the bounded-psh wedge follows inductively from dd^c(G T_Q^{j-1}) by integration by parts and uniform convergence of potentials. The nonpluripolar extension agrees with this local product on T and gives no mass to the toric boundary, which is pluripolar. This justifies all powers used here directly in our C^{1,1} situation.

It follows, when d<n, that
  <T_Q^{d+1}>=0,
and in particular the nonpluripolar n-th power is zero despite the positive kernel-limit mass. Also <T_Q^d> wedged with any smooth omega^{n-d} is locally absolutely continuous with respect to ambient volume on T, since its coefficients there are Hessian minors with locally bounded densities. It therefore gives zero mass to S_Q, whereas mu_Q(S_Q)=d!vol_Lambda(Q)>0. This proves that the kernel limit cannot equal that mixed measure, for any smooth ambient Hermitian omega. Closedness of the ambient form would not repair this mismatch. It is the selection and its intrinsic dimension, not an arbitrary background wedge, that determine the limit.

When d=n, the answer simplifies to the usual closed-curvature interpretation, but here it is proved by explicit Hessians. On r(int Q), the optimizing q is interior, the optimality equation is r=grad F*(q), and G=F. Elsewhere the optimizing q lies in the union of the facets of Q. The Lipschitz map q(r) then has derivative of rank less than n almost everywhere there: on the measurable set where it lies in any fixed facet, the normal component is constant and its derivative is zero almost everywhere on that set. A finite union of facets suffices. Thus
  det D^2 G=1_{grad F(r) in Q} det D^2 F(r) a.e.
The logarithmic-angular normalization of dd^c=(i/(2pi))partial barpartial is
  (dd^c F)^n=n! det D^2 F(r) dr d tau.
The boundary of Q is null and grad F is a diffeomorphism; changing variables q=grad F(r) in the explicit limit yields
  mu_Q=<(theta+dd^c E_Q)^n>.                         (14)
This is the nonpluripolar product, not an undefined ordinary wedge of divisorial currents. For a smooth ambient omega write dvol_omega=a_omega(r,tau)dr d tau on T. The density form of (14) is
  dmu_Q=[n! 1_{grad F(r) in Q} det D^2 F(r)/a_omega(r,tau)]dvol_omega.
Again omega may be nonclosed; theta remains the Chern curvature throughout.

EXPLICIT NON-SUBMERSION, LOWER-GROWTH EXAMPLE. Take n=2, L=O(4,4), product Fubini--Study h, w=0, and
  Q={(2+t,2-t): -1/2<=t<=1/2}.
Its integral affine offset is b=(2,2), W=R(1,-1), Lambda=Z(1,-1), d=1, and dq_Lambda=dt (not sqrt(2)dt). The entire globally selected space is
  V_m=span{z_1^{2m+j} z_2^{2m-j} e^m:
                         j integer, |j|<=m/2}.
Therefore N_m=2 floor(m/2)+1 and the limit mass is 1. Here
  F(r)=4log(1+e^{r_1})+4log(1+e^{r_2}),
  r_1(t)=log((2+t)/(2-t)),   r_2(t)=-r_1(t),
and
  mu_Q=integral_{-1/2}^{1/2}
          [Haar probability on {|z_1|^2=(2+t)/(2-t),
                                |z_2|^2=(2-t)/(2+t)}] dt.
Thus the limit is supported on a compact portion of |z_1 z_2|=1, of real dimension 3, and is singular with respect to any smooth volume on the complex surface. Its potential is explicitly the formula above with
  F*(2+t,2-t)=2c(2+t),
  c(p)=p log(p/4)+(4-p)log((4-p)/4).
Adjacent section ratios are z_1/z_2. The rational map [v_1u_2:u_1v_2], with z_j=v_j/u_j, has indeterminacy at (0,0) and (infinity,infinity); it is not a global submersion on X. The explicit norms concentrate in a transverse radial direction and do not simply integrate against a fixed fiber probability. This shows concretely why this theorem is not just a pullback-submersion model.

One may also make the sampling background genuinely nonclosed in this example. Let omega_0 be the sum of the two Fubini--Study forms, choose a nonconstant smooth torus-invariant f, for instance a nonzero constant times |z_1|^2/(1+|z_1|^2), and put omega=exp(f)omega_0. Then d omega=exp(f)df wedge omega_0 is nonzero where df is nonzero, while omega is a positive smooth Hermitian form. Taking nu=omega^2/integral omega^2 satisfies the theorem. The curvature theta=4omega_0 remains closed, all weighted Hilbert formulas still hold, and the same mass-one shell limit follows.

POSITIVE MASS, EXCEPTIONS, AND SCOPE. Every nonempty Q satisfying the assumptions has positive relative volume and thus positive limiting mass; the singleton case is mass 1. Empty selection, affine lattice congruence obstructions, polytopes touching the box boundary, nonconvex weights, non-invariant sampling or obstacles, and singular or nonpositive sampling densities are not covered. Small degrees may have V_m=0, but the lattice argument guarantees nonzero spaces for all sufficiently large m under the integral-offset hypothesis. No assertion is made for arbitrary compact K, arbitrary selecting series, or the ideal spaces H^0(X,L^m I(m phi)). Proving that a specified ideal series satisfies this exact Newton constraint would be an additional mathematical problem. The theorem above instead supplies a new fully explicit selecting-series class, with global production, all Hilbert-norm changes, the matching envelope lower bound, intrinsic dimension, kernel-measure convergence, and the nonclosed-background relation all proved.

correctness.report:
The theorem correctly applies the declared, verified supports n1 and n2. Their hypotheses are retained: K=X, an interior rational polytope with integral affine offset, smooth invariant sampling with positive density, and a smooth invariant obstacle with strictly positive real Hessian. Thus global production, the entire Newton selection constraint, exact Hilbert norms, Bernstein–Markov, potential convergence, lattice growth and the weak-* kernel limit are established rather than assumed. No identification with the multiplier-ideal envelope is asserted.

The new geometric arguments check out. The inverse gradient restricted to aff Q is an embedding, so the shell Jacobian is smooth and positive and gives the claimed induced-volume density for any Hermitian background. Strong convexity of F* gives the displayed variational inequality and a Lipschitz optimizer q(r); the optimizing-value comparison then gives grad G=q(r). Its almost-everywhere Hessian has range in W. The mollification argument identifies the local wedge products with Hessian minors, so the rank bound annihilates the (d+1)-st power on the torus. Nonpluripolar extension supplies the asserted global conclusion. The mixed d-th measure has locally bounded ambient densities on the torus and therefore cannot equal the positive shell measure when d<n.

For d=n, the facet level-set argument correctly forces rank deficiency almost everywhere outside the interior-optimizer region. Inside that region G=F. With the stated dd^c convention, the factor is exactly n! det(D²F) dr d tau; changing variables by grad F proves the nonpluripolar Monge–Ampère identification and the ambient-volume density formula.

The example has the stated lattice count, lattice volume, conjugate and radii. Its section-ratio map has the two asserted indeterminacy points. The conformally rescaled background is genuinely nonclosed on the surface, while the line-bundle curvature remains closed.

Both summaries accurately describe the scoped theorem and its negative conclusions. The phrase 'support S_Q' is used after explicitly discarding the null relative boundary: S_Q is a full-mass carrier; the topological support is Psi(Q times (S^1)^n). This does not affect any density or singularity assertion. The nonroutine external ingredients underlying the almost-everywhere calculus and canonical nonpluripolar terminology are isolated below; no external kernel-asymptotic theorem is needed.
premises: Rademacher differentiability and level-set calculus: If U is an open subset of R^N and f:U->R^M is locally Lipschitz, then f is differentiable almost everywhere, belongs to W^{1,infinity}_loc(U), and its weak derivative equals its almost-everywhere differential. For a standard smooth compactly supported approximate identity rho_epsilon, D(rho_epsilon*f) converges to Df almost everywhere and in L^p_loc for every 1<=p<infinity. If A is a measurable subset of U and a linear functional lambda:R^M->R satisfies lambda(f(x))=c for all x in A, then lambda composed with Df(x) is zero for almost every x in A.

Nonpluripolar-product locality and extension: Let X be a compact Kahler manifold of complex dimension n, theta a smooth Kahler form, and u a genuine theta-plurisubharmonic function not identically minus infinity. Suppose A is a closed analytic subset of X, u=-infinity on A, and u is locally bounded on X\A. For every 1<=p<=n, the nonpluripolar power <(theta+dd^c u)^p> is a well-defined closed positive (p,p)-current with locally finite mass. On X\A it agrees with the local Bedford–Taylor power. For every smooth Hermitian form beta, its trace measure <(theta+dd^c u)^p> wedge beta^(n-p) gives zero mass to A. Consequently the nonpluripolar power is the trivial extension across A of that local power.

source.report:
Both exact supplied premise strings are established.

Premise 0: [Ern–Guermond, Theorem 2.7](https://people.tamu.edu/~guermond/M661_FALL_2023/chap02.pdf) establishes Rademacher differentiability and equality of classical and weak derivatives. Componentwise application and local Lipschitz bounds give W^{1,∞}_loc membership. Hunter’s [Theorems 1.21 and 1.28](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/pdes/ch1.pdf), together with [Theorem 3.19](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/pdes/ch3.pdf), establish differentiation through mollification and convergence almost everywhere and in every finite local L^p. The measurable-set assertion follows at density points of A: a nonzero differential of λ∘f−c would exclude a cone of positive relative volume from A, contradicting density one. These conclusions apply to the note’s Lipschitz gradient, Hessian mollification and facet arguments.

Premise 1: [BEGZ, Definition 1.1, Proposition 1.6, Theorem 1.8 and the discussion following Definition 1.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0812.3674) establish locally finite mass, positivity, closedness, Bedford–Taylor agreement and trivial extension for the stated setting. Analytic A is locally complete pluripolar. For any smooth Hermitian β, comparison with a Kähler form κ gives β≤Cκ, hence the β-trace is dominated by C^{n−p} times the κ-trace and also gives zero mass to A. Closedness of β is unnecessary. The note applies this on (P¹)^n with closed Kähler Chern curvature; it does not substitute the ambient Hermitian form for that curvature.
